item.title: PNG must prepare early as El Niño risks increase
item.description: Papua New Guinea must strengthen public awareness and prepare early as El Niño conditions continue affecting parts of the country, an official says. President of Farmers and Settlers Association, Wilson Thompson, said changing weather patterns were already being observed, with some areas receiving less rainfall while others experienced only light drizzle.
item.content:encoded:
Papua New Guinea must strengthen public awareness and prepare early as El Niño conditions continue affecting parts of the country, an official says.

President of Farmers and Settlers Association, Wilson Thompson, said changing weather patterns were already being observed, with some areas receiving less rainfall while others experienced only light drizzle.

He said communities needed clear information to prepare for possible dry conditions in the coming months.

“Preparation must begin now,” Thompson said.

He said reports from parts of the country, including Eastern Highlands, showed some rivers and streams were recording lower water levels, while some water sources were beginning to dry up.

Thompson said the prolonged dry weather could affect food production, reduce crop yields and create serious challenges for families who depend on agriculture.

He said limited access to clean water could also increase health risks, including the spread of water-borne diseases such as typhoid and dysentery.

“Public awareness is important. People need to understand how to conserve water, protect food gardens and prevent diseases during dry periods,” he said.

Thompson called on government agencies and provincial administrations to strengthen drought preparedness programs and ensure communities receive timely information.

He said the impact of El Niño could go beyond agriculture, affecting water supplies, household incomes, electricity generation and essential services.

Schools could also face difficulties if access to safe drinking water becomes limited, while farmers should take steps to protect crops, livestock and water sources.

Thompson said stronger coordination between national and provincial authorities was needed to ensure response plans were ready before conditions became worse.

He said lessons from previous droughts, including food security initiatives supported by the National Agricultural Research Institute and other organisations, should guide current preparations.

“We cannot afford to wait. Early preparation and awareness are the best ways to reduce the impact of El Niño on our communities and economy,” Thompson said.

item.title: Hawa CS gets K3m expansion funding
item.description: The Hela Provincial Government has released K3 million to continue construction work at the Hawa Correctional Service facility, the second tranche of funding for the project. Governor Philip Undialu confirmed the release on Wednesday, stating that a total of K10 million has been committed for the development of Hawa CS, which will become the second Highlands Regional Correctional Centre.
item.content:encoded:
The Hela Provincial Government has released K3 million to continue construction work at the Hawa Correctional Service facility, the second tranche of funding for the project.

Governor Philip Undialu confirmed the release on Wednesday, stating that a total of K10 million has been committed for the development of Hawa CS, which will become the second Highlands Regional Correctional Centre.

"Hawa Correctional Service will have three new facilities that will increase capacity, enhance security, and focus on rehabilitation and skills development. The facilities are for high risk, juvenile, and female inmates. Upon completion, holding capacity will increase from current 50 inmates to between 200 - 300 inmates," he said.

Work is currently underway across all three new blocks.

The female wing is progressing with construction of the second storey while Juvenile block has completed first-floor brickwork and is now moving to the second level and the High Risk section has finished ground backfilling and is preparing beam structures and concrete works.

Governor Undialu said over the past three years, the provincial government, in partnership with the National Government, has invested more than K20 million into Hawa CS, with further funding to continue through ongoing activities.

The next phase of the project will shift focus to rehabilitation and reintegration programs.

"Plans are in place to construct a Technical Vocational Education Training and FODE centre at the correctional service. The goal is to ensure prisoners are not merely incarcerated, but are rehabilitated, trained, and equipped with practical skills to return to their communities as productive and responsible citizens," he said.

A proper church facility will also be built within the institution to provide moral guidance, counseling, and spiritual rehabilitation.

The completed facility will feature modern security systems including CCTV surveillance, alarm systems, magnetic doors, secure watchtowers, and separate accommodation for convicted prisoners and remandees.

item.title: MP tells LLG presidents to return to their elected centres
item.description: Delta Fly MP Agena Gamai has called on local level government [LLG] presidents across the district to return to their designated growth centres and serve their communities locally rather than operating out of Balimo, Western. Speaking at the official opening of the new Fly Gogodala LLG chamber in Tapila, Gamai said the official seat of government for each LLG must be respected and utilized effecti
item.content:encoded:
Delta Fly MP Agena Gamai has called on local level government [LLG] presidents across the district to return to their designated growth centres and serve their communities locally rather than operating out of Balimo, Western.

Speaking at the official opening of the new Fly Gogodala LLG chamber in Tapila, Gamai said the official seat of government for each LLG must be respected and utilized effectively by local leadership.

"When you live in Balimo, your councillors and your people will follow you, and when they follow you, they will come with all the demands for their stay in Balimo," he said.

Addressing the Fly Gogodala president directly, the local MP said there was no longer any justification for operating remotely now that dedicated infrastructure has been constructed.

"Fly Gogodala President, now you have no excuse," he said. "You must bring your people back to the seat of government we have already built. Tapila is the seat of government for the Fly Gogodala LLG."

Gamai confirmed that significant funding has been allocated to build out administrative hubs in neighboring LLGs across the district. Tabo LLG received K500,000 to construct its seat of government at Sewase, Aramia Gogodala was also given K500,000 for infrastructure at Awaba, and Wawoi-Guavi LLG also received similar funding to establish its center at Kamusie.

"Presidents, the more you stay in Balimo, the more our people will follow you there," Gamai said. "You are a leader elected and you have responsibility, come back to serve your people here."

Drawing on his own prior experience serving as Bamu LLG president based out of Emeti, Gamai said that modern telecommunications have eliminated the need for local officials to base themselves out of urban hubs like Balimo.

"Today we are connected through communication. You can just communicate from here, not go and stay in Balimo and leave your people," he said.

Gamai also directed LLG managers and public servants to return to their respective stations, stating that once the current round of facility construction concludes, administrative officers will be expected to remain permanently on-site in their districts.

item.title: ‘Drowning in Waste’: Port Moresby’s flooded streets and the Coral Triangle crisis
item.description: In Papua New Guinea’s capital, rising floodwaters are carrying more than rain, they carry the weight of waste, mismanagement, and neglect. An environmental crisis is unfolding across Port Moresby, where the illegal dumping of rubbish and household waste is choking storm drains and triggering chronic urban flooding.
item.content:encoded:
In Papua New Guinea’s capital, rising floodwaters are carrying more than rain, they carry the weight of waste, mismanagement, and neglect.

An environmental crisis is unfolding across Port Moresby, where the illegal dumping of rubbish and household waste is choking storm drains and triggering chronic urban flooding.

What began as a local nuisance has escalated into a major public health hazard and a growing threat to the Coral Triangle, one of the most biodiverse marine regions in the world.

Port Moresby resident Lepi Kari, 48, said the situation has deteriorated significantly over the years as urban development has expanded without adequate drainage upkeep.

"Before, the drainage used to be running and flowing properly, but now with changes taking place here and developments coming up, heavy rain carries debris that blocks off the drains," Kari said.

"NCDC should do something, come clean the drains and let the water flow… when heavy rain falls, it's blocked, causing flooding which spoils our homes and livelihoods. It is always a metre high, and we're always in a pool of water every rainy season. We struggle."

Papua New Guinea relies heavily on imported goods, bringing in hundreds of millions of kina worth of plastic products annually, much of which ultimately ends up as unmanaged waste.

While the National Capital District Commission [NCDC] is tasked with garbage collection, street cleaning, and drain maintenance, service delivery remains inconsistent. Rapid population growth, resource constraints, and unserviced informal settlements have exacerbated the accumulation of waste in public waterways.

For families living in affected communities, the annual wet season brings severe disruption.

"We don’t sit down properly, we don’t sleep properly, the smell is very bad," one local mother said during recent flooding. "I am eating with tears… house is under water. I see the water, I didn’t eat, I just cried and questioned why our homes are underwater."

Beyond the city's suburban streets, local transport operators navigate damaged, flooded roads, while runoff pushes vast quantities of synthetic waste through waterways and into the ocean.

The impacts of Port Moresby's waste crisis extend directly into the ocean. PNG is part of the Coral Triangle alongside Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Timor-Leste, and the Solomon Islands, a region home to 76 per cent of the world's coral species.

Lisa Bun, a Marine Protected Area officer with the Conservation and Environment Protection Authority [CEPA], said plastic pollution is actively suffocating marine ecosystems.

"Plastics do not only affect coral but everything in the ocean," Bun said. "Non-biodegradable plastics don't break down; even if they do, they remain in the environment as microplastics. The obvious impact on coral reefs is that they smother or suffocate them. Corals are animals, so when they suffocate, they die."

She said while national-level discussions on legislation and environmental policies are underway, trans-boundary ocean currents also carry marine debris from neighboring countries into PNG waters, requiring both local and regional action.

In response to the growing crisis, civil society organizations and local youth groups have begun taking action directly.

Civil society group Emplesia Inc, supported by the French Government, recently organized youth volunteers from the Morata Catholic Parish [St Martin De Porres] in Port Moresby's North West electorate to clear choked drainage channels.

Guided by environmental and human rights activist Rosa Koian, the initiative drew inspiration from Pope Francis's environmental encyclical, Laudato Si' , which calls for the protection of the planet.

"What we see is plastic everywhere when we clean," one youth volunteer said. "Boxes and other items decompose, but it's the plastics that are spoiling the drainage. That is why we are cleaning the drains."

A local youth leader emphasized that the problem extends well beyond suburban streets to iconic coastal sites, including Hanuabada and Ela Beach.

"When you go out fishing, it’s hard because plastic has damaged the marine ecosystem, where the fish and sea animals find it difficult to reproduce," the youth leader said. "When we look after the environment by controlling plastic pollution, the environment then takes care of us."

While residents acknowledged routine bag collection efforts by NCDC sanitation workers, community leaders maintain that urgent, systemic action across all levels of government and society is required to address the root causes of urban plastic waste before the damage to local communities and marine ecosystems becomes irreversible.

item.title: Helen Roalakona becomes PNG’s first female Public Prosecutor
item.description: Female Legal eagle Helen Roalakona has made history as Papua New Guinea's first female Public Prosecutor, taking the helm of the country's criminal justice system for a six-year term. Her appointment was confirmed following a rigorous screening and selection process conducted by the Judicial and Legal Services Commission [JLSC], where she emerged as the top candidate.
item.content:encoded:
Female Legal eagle Helen Roalakona has made history as Papua New Guinea's first female Public Prosecutor, taking the helm of the country's criminal justice system for a six-year term.

Her appointment was confirmed following a rigorous screening and selection process conducted by the Judicial and Legal Services Commission [JLSC], where she emerged as the top candidate.

Justice Minister and Attorney-General Pila Niningi commended the appointment, describing it as a landmark moment for gender equality and public sector leadership.

"This is a historic breakthrough for institutional leadership within our justice sector," Mr Niningi said.

He added that Ms Roalakona’s extensive legal background and track record would provide strong, merit-based guidance to the Office of the Public Prosecutor.

Her appointment marks the first time a woman has been selected to lead the statutory office since PNG gained independence.

item.title: Islands Petroleum introduces cleaner diesel fuel option in Lae
item.description: Islands Petroleum has introduced a new fuel product in Lae aimed at supporting modern vehicles, heavy machinery and industrial operations across Papua New Guinea. The company has commissioned a new storage tank at its Lae facility for Ultra Low Sulfur Diesel [ULSD], a cleaner type of diesel fuel with lower sulfur content compared to regular diesel.
item.content:encoded:
Islands Petroleum has introduced a new fuel product in Lae aimed at supporting modern vehicles, heavy machinery and industrial operations across Papua New Guinea.

The company has commissioned a new storage tank at its Lae facility for Ultra Low Sulfur Diesel [ULSD], a cleaner type of diesel fuel with lower sulfur content compared to regular diesel.

Islands Petroleum says the new fuel will help improve engine performance, reduce engine wear and provide customers with a higher-quality fuel option as more businesses invest in modern vehicles and equipment.

Engineering Manager Moses Samo said ULSD contains fewer particles, which helps engines operate more efficiently.

“ULSD is a diesel product with a lower sulfur content in the fuel. A simple way to understand it is that it contains fewer particles, making it better for engines and helping improve engine durability, meaning engines can last longer,” he said.

Samo said fuel can be used in everyday diesel vehicles, but it is especially beneficial for newer trucks, vehicles and heavy equipment that require higher fuel standards.

“This is a higher-specification diesel fuel. It can be used in normal vehicles, but it is especially good for newer vehicles coming into the market, including modern trucks that require efficient and higher-performance fuel,” he said.

Islands Petroleum chief executive officer Nathan Bluett said the investment comes at a time when the global fuel market continues to face uncertainty.

He said international oil prices remain the biggest factor affecting fuel costs.

"We manage fuel supply through a global supply chain and we are subject to global fuel prices. The global oil price is the biggest factor that determines fuel prices,” Bluett said.

He said the new storage facility will improve fuel supply reliability for customers in Lae and the wider region.

The company supplies fuel to several industries, including marine services, trucking, logistics, retail, manufacturing and other industrial operations.

“This project to increase our storage capacity in Lae comes at a time of global fuel uncertainty. This adds further capacity to our storage in Lae and adds to our supply chain reliability,” Bluett said.

Bluett said demand for cleaner fuel is increasing as businesses upgrade their fleets and purchase newer equipment.

“We are seeing growing demand from customers expanding their fleets and investing in newer trucks, vehicles and equipment,” he said.

He added that ULSD gives customers more choices when buying modern vehicles and machinery.

“We want to give our customers the freedom to buy their new fleet, their new truck, or that new piece of equipment that needs the new fuel,” he said.

Islands Petroleum says the ULSD project is part of its wider investment to strengthen fuel storage and supply security in Papua New Guinea.

The company employs more than 600 Papua New Guineans nationwide and says the new fuel product will support the future needs of the transport, mining and industrial sectors by providing a cleaner and more efficient fuel option.

item.title: Port Moresby to face weekend water rationing as court orders unblock critical pipeline repairs
item.description: Water PNG has secured interim National Court orders to proceed with urgent repairs on a primary water pipeline supplying Port Moresby, following a land access dispute that delayed initial works. The National Court at Waigani issued orders restraining the Behori Incorporated Land Group, its members, and agents from blocking access to the Rouna 1/3 raw water pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
Water PNG has secured interim National Court orders to proceed with urgent repairs on a primary water pipeline supplying Port Moresby, following a land access dispute that delayed initial works.

The National Court at Waigani issued orders restraining the Behori Incorporated Land Group, its members, and agents from blocking access to the Rouna 1/3 raw water pipeline.

The critical infrastructure carries approximately half of the capital city's raw water supply. The ruling clears the way for a major partial shutdown of Port Moresby's water supply, now scheduled to run from 10:00pm on Friday, 14 August until 3:00am on Sunday, 16 August.

Water PNG Chief Executive Officer James Young said the city's water supply will be reduced by around half during the repair window, with water rationed across four zones on eight-hour rotations.

"This repair is about preventing something far worse," Young said. "The pipeline is more than sixty years old and it is failing.

"A short, planned, partial shutdown now is how we avoid an uncontrolled burst later, one that could cut more than half the city's water not for a weekend, but for weeks or months, because no spare pipe of this size is held in the country."

Engineers estimate the current leak is losing around 10 million litres of water every day.

Officials warned the wastage poses an immediate risk during an active El Niño period, which is already placing pressure on the Sirinumu catchment - the region's primary source for both drinking water and hydropower.

Water PNG board chairman Meckles Poya welcomed the court's intervention while reaffirming the State Owned Enterprise's intention to maintain a long-term working relationship with traditional landowners.

"We respect the Behori Clan and their deep connection to their land, and at the same time Water PNG has a responsibility under the law to make sure people have safe water," Poya said.

He said Behori-owned contractors had been engaged and paid for preparatory site works, including grading access roads and digging drainage channels, prior to a blockade being erected.

"If the water supply fails, disease can spread, people get sick, and lives can be lost who are often our most vulnerable, our children and the elderly," Poya said.

Water PNG confirmed that full support for the repair program and future pipeline renewal has been backed by the National Government and Kumul Consolidated Holdings.

Detailed zone rationing maps and schedules are expected to be published ahead of the August 14 shutdown.

item.title: North Fly police strengthened with new fleet
item.description: The Police Special Services Division in North Fly will now beef up security operations in the Tabubil mining area and surrounding communities after receiving three new police marked vehicles from Ok Tedi Mining Limited [OTML]. Acting Assistant Commissioner of Police for Border Command Steven Francis said the vehicles will improve police mobility, operational readiness, visibility and response time
item.content:encoded:
The Police Special Services Division in North Fly will now beef up security operations in the Tabubil mining area and surrounding communities after receiving three new police marked vehicles from Ok Tedi Mining Limited [OTML].

Acting Assistant Commissioner of Police for Border Command Steven Francis said the vehicles will improve police mobility, operational readiness, visibility and response times within Tabubil and the wider North Fly area.

The vehicles were officially handed over to police yesterday, and will be assigned to the Special Services Division, whose personnel are regularly deployed to support security operations within the mine’s operational areas.

"This occasion is not simply about the handover of three vehicles. It represents a broader commitment by OTML and the RPNGC Border Command to work together in addressing law-and-order challenges," ACP Francis said.

He said the donation was small but significant as it reflects the continuing strategic partnership between OTML and police.

ACP Francis acknowledged OTML for their continued support to the Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary, particularly provincial commands within the Border Command.

ACP Francis said there has been positive progress through stronger cooperation between OTML, the North Fly Provincial Police Command and the wider RPNGC.

He urged commanders and supervisors to ensure the vehicles are properly registered, monitored, serviced and used only for authorised policing duties.

"These vehicles must be used wisely, maintained properly and deployed in the service of the people. They must not be misused or treated as personal property," he said.

"These assets belong to the people and communities of North Fly. Police officers are only the custodians, and we have a responsibility to protect, maintain and manage them properly."

He thanked OTML for recognising the importance of strengthening police mobility to maintain peace and support the secure operation of one of PNG’s major economic projects.

ACP Francis reaffirmed the Border Command’s commitment to working closely with OTML, communities, government agencies and other partners to improve law enforcement and public safety throughout North Fly and the wider Border Command.

item.title: PNG far below Commonwealth standard for female leaders, former minister says
item.description: PNG political pioneer Lady Carol Kidu is spearheading a national campaign to boost female representation in parliament, urging that the country remains critically short of Commonwealth standards for women in leadership.
